stories.brief: Stef Wertheimer and his push to build Israeli industrial parks and export manufacturing.

sources.title: Stef Wertheimer (1926-) | The National Library of Israel
Billionaire industrialist and philanthropist Stef Wertheimer dies at 98

storyBeats: Stef Wertheimer was born in Germany, and his family moved to Mandatory Palestine in 1937 to escape Nazism.
As a teenager in Tel Aviv, he left school early and learned technical work through apprenticeships and optics study.
During the 1940s he served in British forces and later worked on weapons-related technical work in the Haganah and, after the war, in state defense industry.
In 1952 he founded ISCAR in Nahariya, starting with a small metalworking operation that became the base for his industrial strategy.
He later applied his manufacturing experience to a broader plan: building industrial parks that would cluster factories rather than only individual firms.
Those parks became associated with towns such as Tefen, Omer, Nazareth, and Tel Hai, extending the model beyond a single site.
The industrial-park model was tied to export manufacturing and to Wertheimer’s belief that industry could anchor regional development in northern Israel and elsewhere.
His later plans included cross-border or neighboring-country parks, showing that the industrial-parks concept expanded beyond Israel’s borders.
By the end of his life, Wertheimer was publicly identified as the founder of Israeli industrial parks and a leading advocate of industrial development as a peace-through-prosperity strategy.

stories.brief: Israel Corporation as a state-backed industrial holding company in Israeli business history.
storyBeats: In 1968, Shaul Eisenberg told Finance Minister Pinhas Sapir he was prepared to invest in Israel if the tax problem could be solved.
The Knesset passed a special Israel Corporation law that gave the new company tax relief and made the investment vehicle possible.
Israel Corporation was founded in 1968 as a state-backed vehicle intended to attract foreign capital into the Israeli economy.
The company’s early core holdings included major national assets such as Zim and the oil-refining sector, giving it an outsized role in Israeli industry.
In 1970, Eisenberg became the dominant controlling force in the company, shifting it from a broad investment project into the center of his business empire.
Over the following years, the company expanded through additional Israeli holdings and became a large corporate group with tens of subsidiaries and major employment reach.

The company’s control structure was routed through foreign-registered holding entities, reflecting both its international financing design and the limits of Israel’s investment environment at the time.
By the early 1980s, Eisenberg was removed from the executive committee in a power struggle involving other investors and Bank Hapoalim figures.
After Eisenberg’s death, the family’s stake was sold to the Ofer family in 1999, ending the Eisenberg era and opening a new ownership chapter.
Israel Corporation later remained a major Israeli industrial holding, but its historical significance came to rest on the earlier state-backed creation, asset buildup, and ownership battles.

stories.brief: The Railway Queen tradition tied to Britain’s Stockton and Darlington centenary.

sources.title: Commemorating the past, shaping the future: the jubilee and centenary celebrations of the Stockton and Darlington Railway
‘This modern Cinderella’: Railway Queens, mass media, and British civic culture, 1925–75
Railway Queens and The Mid Cheshire Line

storyBeats: The Stockton and Darlington Railway centenary in 1925 was planned as a large public commemoration of the line’s 1825 opening, with a parade, exhibition, and civic ceremony centered on Darlington and nearby railway works.
As part of that centenary season, organizers created the first Railway Queen crowning, selecting a young woman from a railway-family background to represent the railway celebrations.
The first Railway Queen was Helena Wotton, also referred to in later accounts as Ella Wotton, and contemporary and later sources place her crowning on 27 September 1925.

The centenary pageant did not remain a single local spectacle: the Railway Queen idea became the template for a broader British ‘Queens of Industry’ practice that spread into other sectors in the following years.
Early Railway Queens were typically daughters of railway workers and were often teenagers, which made the role both a publicity device and a worker-family showcase rather than a formal office.
The Railway Queen model continued beyond 1925, with later queens appearing at railway carnivals and representing the industry in public events, including travel and official visits.

By 1928 and 1935, Railway Queens were being used in more elaborate promotional settings, including overseas visits and large-scale carnival ceremonies, showing that the centenary experiment had become an established tradition.

The tradition lasted into the later twentieth century and ended with the final Railway Queen crowning at Shildon in 1975, closing a fifty-year run that began with the Stockton and Darlington centenary.

stories.brief: Naomi Shemer as a major Israeli songwriter, poet, and cultural figure.
storyBeats: Naomi Shemer emerged as one of the central Israeli songwriters of the state’s early decades, working in Hebrew popular song and children’s music.
She wrote songs that entered the core repertoire of Israeli culture, including works performed by leading singers and broadcast widely.
Her writing moved between intimate lyricism, collective memory, and national themes, which made her songs usable in schools, ceremonies, and radio programming.
Jerusalem of Gold became her best-known song and turned her into a nationally recognized figure after the Six-Day War.
The song’s success made Shemer a public cultural authority, and later generations continued to treat her work as part of the country’s shared vocabulary.
She kept composing new songs and adapting literary and folk material into Hebrew verse, extending her reach beyond a single signature hit.
Her work also became tied to musical performance by prominent Israeli artists, which helped fix her songs in mainstream memory.
She periodically faced disputes over authorship and political meaning attached to her songs, especially when later audiences read them in new historical contexts.
By the time of her death in 2004, she had become one of the canonical Israeli cultural figures whose songs remained in circulation long after their first performance.
The National Library of Israel continues to preserve and present her materials as part of the broader archive of Israeli music history.

Chaim Topol’s breakthrough from Israeli stage work to international screen roles.

sources.title: Chaim Topol’s Unbelievable Journey to "Fiddler on the Roof"
Sallah Shabati / film by Ephraim Kishon
How the late actor Topol turned Tevye into a Zionist

storyBeats: Chaim Topol began his entertainment career while serving in the Nahal military troupe, where he also met his wife.
His comic performance as Sallah Shabati onstage and in the film version gave him his first major breakthrough in Israel.
That role also risked typecasting him as a mimic and comic actor in the Israeli press and public eye.
He later played Tevye in the Israeli stage production of Fiddler on the Roof, initially sharing the role with Shmuel Rodensky.
A television appearance with Danny Kaye helped move Topol from Israeli stage recognition to international attention.
After that exposure, he won the role of Tevye in the 1971 film adaptation of Fiddler on the Roof.
The film made him internationally famous and fixed Tevye as the role most associated with him.
The National Library archive also preserves Topol materials and documents his later public memory in Israel.
Topol’s career left a two-track legacy: a major Israeli comedic breakthrough and an enduring global identification with Fiddler on the Roof.

stories.brief: Strauss Group’s rise from a confectionery business into a major Israeli food producer.
storyBeats: The Strauss story began in Nahariya in the 1930s, when Richard and Hilda Strauss set up a small family dairy.
The business started with a very small herd and a simple dairy operation rather than an industrial plant.
Over time the family enterprise expanded from dairy basics into branded consumer foods and larger-scale production.
A major step came in 1979, when Strauss began producing Milky, which became its most successful chilled dairy dessert.
The company later merged its dairy and fresh-food activities into a broader group structure.
Strauss also expanded into salads, juices, chocolate, and other food categories, moving far beyond the original dairy business.
The company’s internal history and National Library records preserve the family and corporate memory of that expansion.
Strauss became one of Israel’s best-known food companies, with a broad consumer-food portfolio rather than a single dairy line.
Its later corporate identity linked food production with Israeli agricultural sourcing and food-tech activity.

stories.brief: Lotte Reiniger’s silhouette animation as an early film-art tradition.
storyBeats: Lotte Reiniger was born in Berlin in 1899 and became interested in silhouettes and shadow theater as a young artist.
In 1919 she co-founded the Institut für Kulturforschung in Berlin, which became an early base for her film work.
She developed silhouette paper-cut animation as her distinctive cinematic method and made it her own.
Her first film work included title silhouettes for Paul Wegener’s films before she moved into her own directing and animation practice.
In 1926 she released The Adventures of Prince Achmed, identified as the first feature-length animated film to survive.
That film established her reputation in animation history and remains a reference point for early feature animation.
She moved to London in 1935 and eventually settled there in 1949, continuing animation work in Britain.
Her archive preserves drawings, designs, letters, and film-related objects that document the practical methods behind her work.
Reiniger became recognized as a pioneer who helped define silhouette animation as a film art form.

stories.brief: A neighbor invites another resident to a small community garden behind the building to compare seedlings and trade extra pots. One person brings herbs that grew well on the balcony, while the other has too many tomato seedlings and not enough sunny space. They talk about what will survive in shade, ask a practical question about watering, and notice that one planter needs better soil before the next week. After a short discussion, they divide the plants, add labels, and decide to water together on Saturday morning. In the end, both people leave with healthier pots, a simple shared plan, and a reason to keep checking on the garden.
